reference.source: Resnick's Diagnosis of Bone and Joint Disorders / GeneReviews
clinicalPearls: A benign high-bone-mass disorder characterised by endosteal thickening of the long-bone cortices and dense sclerosis of the skull, often an incidental finding
Caused by gain-of-function variants in LRP5, a WNT co-receptor, which enhance WNT/beta-catenin signalling and drive increased bone formation
Inherited in an autosomal dominant manner and typically associated with a torus palatinus, a broad or prominent jaw and increased bone density on imaging
Individuals are usually asymptomatic and notably resistant to fractures despite the markedly raised bone density
Bone density measurement shows strikingly elevated values, and the condition is a recognised cause of dense bones without fragility
Cranial-nerve compression is uncommon in the Worth type, distinguishing it from more aggressive sclerosing dysplasias, though skull thickening should still be monitored
Management is generally observation, with attention to any rare cranial-nerve symptoms and reassurance about the excellent bone strength
reference.pathophysiology: Worth endosteal hyperostosis is caused by activating (gain-of-function) variants in LRP5, a co-receptor in the canonical WNT/beta-catenin pathway that is central to osteoblast activity and bone accrual. The variants impair the ability of natural inhibitors such as sclerostin to switch off signalling, so WNT-driven bone formation is persistently enhanced. The result is dense, thickened cortices from endosteal apposition and a sclerotic skull, but with structurally sound bone that resists fracture. Because the excess bone deposition is comparatively orderly and rarely encroaches severely on cranial foramina in this type, most affected individuals remain asymptomatic apart from the characteristic jaw prominence and torus palatinus.
additionalDifferentials: Van Buchem disease and sclerosteosis (SOST-related high bone mass)
Fluorosis or other causes of diffusely dense bone
additionalInvestigations: Plain radiographs showing endosteal cortical thickening and cranial sclerosis
Bone densitometry documenting the markedly increased bone mineral density
Skull imaging to assess vault thickening and screen for foraminal narrowing
Biochemical bone profile to exclude other causes of sclerosis
LRP5 molecular genetic testing to confirm the gain-of-function variant
Family assessment given the autosomal dominant inheritance
redFlags: Progressive hearing loss, visual disturbance or facial weakness suggesting cranial-nerve compression from skull thickening
Atypical fractures or bone pain prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis
Rapidly progressive craniofacial overgrowth pointing to a more aggressive sclerosing dysplasia
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is excellent with a normal life expectancy and bones that are resistant rather than prone to fracture; serious complications from cranial-nerve compression are uncommon in the Worth type.
pitfalls: Confusing the benign high bone mass with osteopetrosis or a symptomatic sclerosing dysplasia and over-investigating
Assuming dense bones imply fragility when LRP5 high bone mass is characteristically fracture-resistant
Neglecting periodic cranial-nerve and hearing assessment despite the generally benign course
Failing to recognise the autosomal dominant pattern and counsel relatives
references: Resnick's Diagnosis of Bone and Joint Disorders
management: Reassure that this is a benign high-bone-mass disorder with fracture-resistant bone requiring no bone-directed drug therapy
Avoid antiresorptive and bone-forming agents, which are unnecessary and inappropriate given the already elevated bone density
Monitor skull and cranial vault thickening clinically and radiologically for the uncommon possibility of cranial-nerve compression
Refer for surgical decompression only if foraminal narrowing produces cranial-nerve deficits
Provide dental and maxillofacial assessment for symptomatic torus palatinus or jaw prominence
Confirm the diagnosis with LRP5 molecular genetic testing and offer genetic counselling given autosomal dominant inheritance
Screen at-risk family members and distinguish the disorder from more aggressive sclerosing dysplasias
